newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS - Riksbank cuts repo, inflation outlook upbeat.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Riksbank cuts repo, inflation outlook upbeat.

text.p: Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank, on Tuesday ended 1996 with an upbeat inflation report which coincided with the 25th cut this year in the bank's key interest rate, the repo.
As the Riksbank cut the rate by 25 basis points to 4.10 percent, the bank released its final inflation report for the year saying the outlook for inflation over the next two years was good.
But the central bank added a warning about wage rises which are seen as the main source of potential inflation.

"The outlook for inflation is somewhat more optimistic than in the report last September," the Riksbank said in a statement, forecasting inflation rates of 1.5 percent in 1997 and two percent in 1998. The current annual rate is just under one percent.
It said data since September had brightened the picture.
"The main factors have been strongly rising exports and investment," the bank said.
"Still it is not considered likely that in the coming two years economic activity will rise above the level of resource utilisation at which inflation is liable to pick up."
Economists saw the upbeat report as indication of further cuts in the repo rate, the bank's key tool for controlling money market liquidity, that was 8.91 percent in January 1996.

Tuesday's cut was widely expected by the markets, especially after figures last week showed a drop of 0.3 percent in November's consumer price index, indicating a negative annual inflation trend for the second consecutive month.
"The rate cut was expected and market reaction was calm," said Knut Hallberg, Swedbank analyst.
Economists forecast further cuts early in 1997 while the Riksbank said additional room for lowering the repo further was now limited.
"I expect the next lowering to be in January and that the Riksbank will then choose to lower the repo rate by 25 basis points again," said Handelsbanken economist Jan Haggstrom.
Richard Woodworth, European economist at Merrill Lynch, said he saw the repo bottoming at about 3.75 percent.
"There's probably still room left, but given the assessment of the economy and the fact that the recovery should be gaining pace next year, we don't expect dramatic easing," Woodworth told Reuters.
Riksbank deputy governor Lars Heikensten told a press conference: "We have lowered rates so much that it is obvious that we will gradually come closer to the bottom."
In its inflation report, the Riksbank said the rate of inflation in 1996 was expected to be some tenths of a percentage point below its target's lower tolerance level.
The central bank's target has been for two percent with a one percentage point movement in either direction.
"This largely stems from transitory effects of decreased interest costs and lower import prices," the bank said.
"These tendencies reflect an enhancement of economic policy's credibility."
However the bank warned if wage increases in 1997 and 1998 were as high as in 1996, when wages are expected to rise six to seven percent, the rate of inflation could pass the target.
